tracks.title: New York State of Mind
tracks.note: Two names turn a city-wide homecoming into something local: Chinatown downtown, Riverside on the west side.

tracks.title: The 59th Street Bridge Song (Feelin' Groovy)
tracks.note: The bridge is in the title. The song itself stays with the pace of a morning walk, giving a familiar crossing a different tempo.

tracks.title: Chelsea Hotel #2
tracks.album: New Skin for the Old Ceremony
tracks.note: A specific hotel becomes the setting for a private memory. The title keeps that memory attached to West 23rd Street.

tracks.title: Cornelia Street
tracks.note: A short street carries the weight of a relationship. This entry follows the street named in the song, without turning a private home into a destination.

tracks.title: 53rd & 3rd
tracks.note: The title reads like directions: one cross street, one avenue. It gives this Midtown corner a very different identity from the office blocks around it.

tracks.title: Across 110th Street
tracks.note: The street works as a boundary in the title of this soul soundtrack recording. Here the map stays with the named street, rather than inventing a single scene.

tracks.title: Spanish Harlem
tracks.note: The neighborhood gives the song its name. Its image of a rose is intimate, but it does not identify a real flower bed to visit.

tracks.title: Bleecker Street
tracks.excerpt: Like a shroud, it covers Bleecker Street
tracks.note: Fog, rented rooms and voices from a café give the street a lived-in texture. The named street is certain; the café remains unnamed.

tracks.title: Coney Island Baby
tracks.note: Lou Reed puts Coney Island in the title of a song about belonging. The place is a broad association, not a set of directions to one attraction.

tracks.title: No Sleep Till Brooklyn
tracks.note: Brooklyn is the destination. Keeping the whole borough on the map is more faithful to the title than selecting an arbitrary club or street.

tracks.title: 52nd Street
tracks.note: A named Manhattan street anchors the title track of the album. The words turn rhythm and a little parade into a street-level image.

tracks.title: Talkin' New York
tracks.excerpt: I landed up on the downtown side / Greenwich Village
tracks.note: A subway ride brings the narrator to Greenwich Village and a search for work in coffee houses. The lyric names the neighborhood directly.

tracks.title: Tompkins Square Park
tracks.note: The East Village park becomes a meeting place at the edge of a breakup. The park is named; no particular bench or entrance is identified.

tracks.title: Washington Square
tracks.note: A banjo-led instrumental carries the name of the Greenwich Village park. First released in 1963, it appears here on a later digital edition.

tracks.title: Central Park West
tracks.note: Coltrane gives this quiet instrumental the name of the avenue along the park. Its connection is in the title, without a lyric or a specific building.

tracks.title: Central Park Blues (2021 - Stereo Remaster)
tracks.note: Simone lets the piano do the describing. Central Park appears in the title of this instrumental, without naming a path, lawn or landmark inside it.

tracks.title: Harlem
tracks.note: Summer heat, winter cold, Saturday nightlife and Sunday morning unfold in the same neighborhood. Withers keeps returning to Harlem as daily life changes around it.

tracks.title: Harlem Shuffle
tracks.note: Harlem enters through the name of a dance. This Rolling Stones recording of the song belongs to the neighborhood-level map, without assigning its dance floor to a particular club.

tracks.title: Drop Me off in Harlem (feat. Duke Ellington and His Orchestra)
tracks.album: Ella Fitzgerald Sings: The Duke Ellington Songbook (Expanded Edition)
tracks.note: Fitzgerald sings the neighborhood as a destination, accompanied by Ellington and his orchestra. The title asks for Harlem as a whole, rather than one doorstep.

tracks.title: On Broadway
tracks.note: Bright lights and the hope of making a living turn Broadway into a test of ambition. The map uses a representative point in the theater district.

tracks.title: Rockaway Beach
tracks.note: A beach escape gives this fast, compact Ramones song its destination. It adds the Atlantic edge of Queens to the collection without pretending to identify one stretch of sand.

tracks.title: Funkin' for Jamaica
tracks.note: Jamaica here is the Queens neighborhood where Browne grew up. Trumpet, keyboards and vocals make a neighborhood tribute, with no individual house pinned.

tracks.title: Queens Get the Money
tracks.note: The borough is right in the title. This entry stays at that scale rather than substituting Queensbridge or a personal address for the wider place Nas names.

tracks.title: South Bronx (Live at SOB's, NYC, NY - 1990)
tracks.note: The South Bronx is the declaration at the center of the song. This is the live recording at SOB’s included on Live Hardcore Worldwide; the mapped place is the South Bronx, not the performance venue.

tracks.title: Brooklyn Baby
tracks.note: Brooklyn becomes part of a carefully performed identity. The title names the borough; it does not supply a particular apartment, club or street.

tracks.title: Brooklyn Zoo
tracks.album: The Definitive Ol' Dirty Bastard Story (Remastered)
tracks.note: Brooklyn gives the song its name and force. This entry keeps the title association at borough scale. First released in 1995, the selected recording comes from a later remastered compilation.

tracks.title: Staten Island Groove
tracks.note: An instrumental brings Staten Island into the record collection through its title. The map shows the borough, without inventing a ferry, venue or street connection.

tracks.title: Bronx Blues
tracks.album: Stan Getz And The Oscar Peterson Trio
tracks.note: The Bronx gets a jazz entry as well as a hip-hop one. This instrumental names the borough without supplying a smaller destination.

tracks.title: Manhattan
tracks.album: Ella Fitzgerald Sings The Rodgers And Hart Song Book
tracks.note: Rodgers and Hart’s city song gives Fitzgerald a whole borough to sing about. This entry follows the title at that broad scale, leaving its many possible stops open.

tracks.title: Lullaby of Birdland
tracks.note: The standard takes its name from the New York jazz club. The map refers to the original Broadway location associated with the song, rather than the later West 44th Street venue.

tracks.title: Take the 'A' Train
tracks.excerpt: To go to Sugar Hill way up in Harlem.
tracks.note: The Ellington Uptown recording includes vocals by Betty Roché. The song’s subway directions lead to Sugar Hill in Harlem; the map shows that neighborhood rather than a private home.

tracks.title: coney island (feat. The National)
tracks.note: Swift and the National return to Coney Island as a place of regret and absence. It shares the same neighborhood entry as Lou Reed, without identifying a real bench from the lyric.

tracks.title: Ludlow St.
tracks.note: Casablancas connected this song to a changing Lower East Side in his Pitchfork interview. The street becomes a way to ask whether a familiar neighborhood still feels like home.

tracks.title: Bleecker & MacDougal
tracks.note: Two street names make the title unusually precise. The map marks their Greenwich Village intersection, without claiming that a particular cafe is the song’s setting.

tracks.title: Brooklyn Bridge To Chorus
tracks.note: The bridge appears in the title, where a physical crossing sits beside a musical one. This entry makes no claim that the recording or music video was made on the bridge.

tracks.title: Lullaby of Broadway
tracks.note: Doris Day gives Broadway a different hour and tempo from the Drifters. Both songs share the same representative theater-district location; neither entry claims one named theater.
